records.name_note: NC State's dedicated Perilla frutescens page lists three common names, Beefsteak Plant, Perilla and Shiso, with Beefsteak Plant first. Its description opens 'Beefsteak plant is a flowering, annual, edible in the Lamiaceae (mint) family...'.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's dedicated Perilla frutescens page, in its "Insects, Diseases, and Other Plant Problems" paragraph, says: "No serious insect or disease problems. It can be toxic to cattle." The only animal named is cattle. The page carries no Poison block and no Problem-for-Cats or Problem-for-Dogs tags, so there is no cat or dog evidence either way. The cattle statement is not extended to cats, dogs or horses. No poison-part list, symptom list or handling warning is given. The Problems field on the same page lists Invasive Species and Weedy. Edibility on the same page: "Leaves as a salad herb, flavoring" (Edibility field); "The seeds are often harvested for human consumption." (Uses (Ethnobotany) field); the Plant Type field includes Edible. No preparation times or conditions are given for eating it.
unknowns: Only NC State (plants.ces.ncsu.edu) has a dedicated, loadable page for Perilla frutescens among the admissible sources. The RHS and Clemson URLs I tried returned 404 or 403, MoBot's plantfinder.mobot.org would not connect, and UF/IFAS EDIS errored. No other dedicated page was found, so every populated field rests on NC State alone.

toxic_to_pets is null: the only toxicity evidence on the dedicated page is 'It can be toxic to cattle.' It names no cat or dog evidence. Other admissible UGA/UF pages mention perilla mint only inside multi-species pasture and horse-toxin pages, which are not dedicated pages for this taxon and were not used. The perilla ketone mechanism and horse toxicity are therefore not recorded here.

is_edible is true but conditional on part: NC State lists leaves as a salad herb and flavoring and says the seeds are often harvested for human consumption, while the same page says the plant can be toxic to cattle. It gives no preparation instructions, quantities or safety limits for people.

NC State states the plant is invasive in North Carolina and is listed as invasive in VA, WV, TN and KY. It self-seeds prolifically with wind-dispersed seeds, and the page advises pinching off flowers before seed set to slow spread. This matters for planting decisions but has no schema field.

is_houseplant false: no admissible source frames it as a houseplant. NC State treats it as an outdoor annual herb (Plant Type: Annual, Edible, Herb, Herbaceous Perennial, Weed; USDA zones 10a-11b) and says nothing about indoor culture.

chill_damage_f is null: NC State's 'USDA Plant Hardiness Zone: 10a, 10b, 11a, 11b' is a hardiness listing, not a damage-onset temperature. It is also odd for an annual, and it was not used for any temperature field.

Day and night temperature, humidity, indoor light (fc) and direct_sun_hours_max are null. NC State's Resistance To Challenges list names Heat, Drought, Dry Soil and Humidity as tolerances only, and its Light field gives only the site-wide category legend for hours.

water_regime and the other watering fields are null: NC State gives no watering instruction. The 'moist to dry soil' and 'drought tolerant' wording describes soil and tolerance, not a watering regime.
soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max are null: NC State gives no pH on this page.
Fertilizer fields are null: no admissible source says anything about fertilizing it.
attracts_pollinators is null: NC State's page has no Attracts field and no pollinator statement.

Sun exposure full_sun and part_shade come from NC State's structured Light field and its 'full sun to partial shade' prose. Its Soil Drainage field (Good Drainage, Occasionally Wet) maps to moderate. Soil base garden_bed is my reading of an in-ground annual grown in 'rich' soil, and no source names a soil mix.

NC State's Plant Type field renders five values: Annual, Edible, Herb, Herbaceous Perennial, Weed. Its Life Cycle field says Annual. The page's own 'Herbaceous Perennial' plant-type value conflicts with that, and I did not resolve it.

Mature size is from NC State's Dimensions block: Height 1 ft 0 in to 3 ft 0 in (12-36 in) and Width 0 ft 3 in to 1 ft 6 in (3-18 in). The description prose agrees ('up to 3 feet tall and 1 1/2 feet wide').

records.name_note: Only one admissible source's dedicated page for this exact taxon could be retrieved (NC State); RHS, MoBot, Clemson and UF/IFAS pages could not be retrieved (see unknowns), so no source split could be tested. NC State's page-title parenthetical is an alphabetized list (Blue Sailors, Chicory, Coffeeweed, Common Chicory, Cornflower, Italian Dandelion, Succory), in the same order as its rendered Common Name(s) list, whose first entry is Blue Sailors; Chicory was chosen because the page's Description opens with "Chicory". Cornflower appears in that list, but NC State also uses that name for a different species, Centaurea cyanus (its page lists Bachelor's Button, Bachelors Buttons, Bluebottle, Cornflower, and its Description says "Cornflower is a hardy, low maintenance cool season annual"; that species is already in this catalog as Bachelor's Button), so it is not used as a display name here. Cichorium endivia (Endive) is a separate species with its own NC State page (Batavia, Endive, Escarole, Frisée) and is kept as its own record; the chicory page has an "often confused with" module, lists Belgian Endive, French Endive and Radicchio under var. foliosum of chicory, and says Cichorium endivia is the salad green known as curly endive. Italian Dandelion is a listed common name of this species.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's chicory page carries no Poison block and no Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tags, so no toxicity statement is recorded. Edibility as written by NC State (Edibility field): "Leaves can be used in salads or cooked to reduce bitter flavor. Roots can be dried and used as a coffee substitute. Flowers are edible." Description adds: "Edible, though bitter, rough hairy leaves resemble dandelion leaves appear in a rosette its first year." and "The roots are also edible and are often dried, ground and used as a coffee substitute." The page gives no forcing or blanching instructions and no times or temperatures for cooking.
unknowns: Only NC State Plant Toolbox had a retrievable dedicated page. RHS (rhs.org.uk/plants/cichorium-intybus and a chicory/cichorium-intybus/details path) returned a 404 or generic non-plant page; Clemson HGIC returned 403; MoBot plantfinder/missouribotanicalgarden.org, UF/IFAS EDIS and ask.ifas were denied or unreachable from the sandbox; no Penn State, UMD or UGA page was found. Nothing was borrowed from them.

Weediness as written by NC State: "While it can be weedy, it does not frequently invade natural habitats." and "It is weedy in fields, pastures, and along roadsides and considered invasive in some states." The page's Problems field is Weedy, and its tags include #edible weed, #lawn weed and #roadside.
toxic_to_pets left null: the NC State page has no Poison block and no cat/dog tags, and no other admissible source was retrieved.

is_edible is true, with the conditions the source gives: leaves can be used in salads or cooked to reduce bitter flavor (no time given), roots dried and used as a coffee substitute, flowers edible. The page says leaves are bitter. No forcing or blanching conditions are stated. Radicchio and Belgian endive are listed as var. foliosum cultivars and the page says they are very different from the parent plant; their culture is not recorded here.

NC State size conflict: the structured Dimensions block gives Height 3 ft. 0 in. - 4 ft. 0 in. and Width 1 ft. 6 in. - 2 ft. 0 in. (used here), while the Description prose says it grows typically 2 to 4 feet tall and 1 foot wide.
Life cycle on NC State is listed as both Biennial and Perennial, and Plant Type lists Annual and Herbaceous Perennial; the Description calls it a biennial.

soil_ph_max left null: NC State lists Alkaline (>8.0) as well as Neutral (6.0-8.0), and the alkaline band is open-ended, so no ceiling. soil_ph_min 6.0 is the closed lower edge of the Neutral band; no Acid band is listed.

soil_drainage moderate rests on NC State's Soil Drainage tags Good Drainage, Moist and Occasionally Dry; the Description also says it prefers well-drained soil and is quite drought tolerant once established.

water_regime left null: no watering statement, only drought-tolerance and soil-moisture tags. soil_base left null: no source states a potting or bed medium in the enum's terms. Temperature, humidity, fertilizer and indoor light fields left null: no admissible support. The Description says it does not do well in heat and humidity and can suffer in southern summers, which is not a humidity percentage.
direct_sun_hours_max left null: NC State's 'Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)' is the site-wide light-category legend text, not species-specific prose.
USDA zones 3a-8b and NC regions Coastal/Mountains/Piedmont are on the page but are regional range ratings, not chill-damage figures; chill_damage_f left null.

is_houseplant false: no admissible source frames it as a houseplant. NC State's Plant Type field lists Annual, Edible, Herbaceous Perennial, Vegetable, Weed and Wildflower, and it gives USDA zones 3a-8b and calls it weedy in fields, pastures and along roadsides.

records.name_note: Admissible sources split on the primary common name, and "European Hazelnut" is not the lead name on either dedicated page. NC State's page title parenthetical lists Cobnut, European Filbert, European Hazel, Filbert, Harry Lauder's Walking Stick, Hazelnut (an alphabetized list, first entry Cobnut), while its Description prose says the shrub is commonly known as the European Hazel. RHS's page title for Corylus avellana (F) leads with "hazel", and "European hazelnut" and "cobnut" appear in its "Other common names" list. Cobnut was chosen because it is the first item of NC State's list and also appears in RHS's other-names list. MoBot could not be loaded, so it was not consulted.
unknowns: MoBot Plant Finder page for Corylus avellana (taxonid=277826) failed to load repeatedly (ConnectError), so nothing was taken from it. No dedicated page for this species was found on Clemson, UF/IFAS, PSU, UMD or UGA in a search.
No admissible source gives a toxicity statement for this taxon, so toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail are null. NC State shows no Poison block on this page.

Edibility: NC State says hazelnuts (cobnuts) are edible, but also says the varieties or cultivars found in the US are typically lacking the desired taste and are roasted and eaten by some. RHS's description says the shrub's catkins are followed by edible nuts in autumn.

Pollinators: NC State's structured Attracts field lists only Songbirds; the true value rests on the Wildlife Value prose saying bees are attracted to the pollen. RHS has no pollinator tag on its page.

Size: NC State gives 12-20 ft tall and 8-15 ft wide (144-240 in and 96-180 in), used as the anchor. RHS gives Max Height 4-8 metres and Max Spread 4-8 metres (157.5-315 in), which differs, with a 5-10 year time to maturity.
outdoor_sun_exposure: NC State lists Full sun and Partial Shade (2-6 hours of direct sun); RHS lists Full sun, Partial shade. Both map to full_sun and part_shade.

soil_ph_max is null: NC State lists Alkaline (>8.0), an open-ended band, and RHS lists Alkaline or Neutral, so no ceiling is supported. soil_ph_min 6.0 is the floor of NC State's Neutral (6.0-8.0) band, and no acid band is listed.

water_regime is null: both sources give only soil-moisture adjectives (NC State Moist, RHS moist but well-drained), not a watering statement. All other watering and fertilizing fields are null for lack of species-specific advice.

is_houseplant false: no admissible source frames it as a houseplant; NC State's Plant Type field lists Shrub and Tree and it gives USDA zones 4a-8b. Temperature, humidity, indoor light and chill damage are null for lack of any figure in the sources read.
soil_base garden_bed reflects an in-ground shrub with the NC State soil textures listed; no source names a potting mix.

records.toxicity_detail: RHS (Potentially harmful field): "Harmful if eaten; fruit/flowers edible if cooked. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling". RHS also carries the line "Pets (dogs, cats): Harmful if eaten; fruit/flowers edible if cooked - for further information and contact numbers regarding pets, see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants". RHS states no part list and no symptoms. NC State's Poisonous to Humans block (human-scoped, not a cat/dog rating) gives Poison Severity Medium (the page also says "This plant has medium severity poison characteristics."), Poison Symptoms "feeling ill, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea", Poison Toxic Principle "cyanide-inducing glycosides", Causes Contact Dermatitis "No", Poison Part: Leaves, Roots, Seeds, Stems. NC State carries no Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tag on this page (its Problems field lists Malodorous, Weak Wood, Weedy). Sources differ on scope and edibility: NC State's poison parts do not list the fruit, and NC State describes the black fruits as edible (pies, wines, jellies; berries made into jam and syrup) with no cooking condition and also carries the tag #edible leaves although Leaves is a listed poison part, whereas RHS says fruit/flowers are edible only if cooked and gives an unscoped harmful-if-eaten warning. Neither source distinguishes ripe from unripe berries; RHS's only condition is that fruit/flowers are edible if cooked, and NC State states no cooking condition.

records.toxicity_detail: No admissible source (NC State Plant Toolbox, Missouri Botanical Garden, RHS) carries a Poison block, a toxicity statement, or a Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tag for Castanea mollissima, so no toxicity rating is recorded. This is Castanea, not horse chestnut/buckeye (Aesculus); no buckeye toxicity is applied. Handling warning (NC State, Description): "The nut is edible, attracts wild life, but use caution when handling it because it is spiny." The nuts are encased in spiny burs (NC State Fruit Description: "Edible chestnuts are encased in spiny dehiscent burs (2 to 3 inches in diameter), usually 2 to 3 nuts per bur."). Preparation as stated by NC State: Uses (Ethnobotany) "The nut is edible raw, boiled, or baked."; Edibility "Seeds can be baked and consumed."; Fruit Description "It is good for fresh-eating, roasting, boiling and baking." MoBot (Uses) mentions harvesting the chestnuts for roasting. NC State Plant Type values: Edible, Perennial, Tree; tags include #edible nuts, #children's garden, #playground plant, #wildlife friendly; Problems: Messy (NC State: "However, falling chestnuts can pose a litter problem."). NC State Play Value lists Edible fruit, Pieces Used in Games, Textural, and Landscape Location includes Recreational Play Area. Edibility is stated for the nut/seed only; no source addresses eating other parts.
unknowns: name_note left null: NC State, MoBot and RHS all lead with Chinese chestnut, no split.

toxic_to_pets left null: none of the admissible pages (NC State, MoBot, RHS) mentions toxicity to cats, dogs or any animal; no Poison block or Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tag exists on the NC State page. The spiny-bur handling warning is recorded in toxicity_detail only.

is_edible is true for the nut/seed only. NC State says the nut is edible raw, boiled, or baked and the seeds can be baked and consumed; MoBot and NC State mention roasting. No source addresses eating any other part of the tree.

outdoor_sun_exposure is full_sun only. NC State's Light field also lists 'Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours)' and its prose says 'prefers full sun to partial shade', but MoBot's structured Sun field lists Full sun only and its Culture text says full sun, so part_shade was dropped. RHS carries no sun field.
direct_sun_hours_max left null: the only hour figures are in NC State's site-wide light legend, which is not species-specific.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max left null: NC State lists both Acid (<6.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0), and its Acid band is open-ended; the Neutral band's closed top of 8.0 is not used as a ceiling, and RHS carries no pH field to cross-check. NC State prose says it does well in neutral and mildly acidic conditions.

water_regime left null: NC State has no watering statement beyond soil description (moist well drained soil, tolerates occasional drought); MoBot structured Water is Medium, which is mid-scale and does not support keep_moist. Culture says established trees do well in dry conditions.

Size: NC State Dimensions block (Height 40-60 ft, Width 40-60 ft) is used, converted to 480-720 in. MoBot structured Height and Spread also say 40 to 60 feet, but NC State's Description prose says about 40 feet height and spread, and MoBot prose says typically 40 ft, less frequently to 60 ft.

RHS has a dedicated species page (Name Status Correct, family Fagaceae, plant range Far East) but it carries no size, sun, soil, hardiness, or care fields, so it supplies only name evidence. Clemson HGIC, UF/IFAS (chestnut production publication HS1155 and gall wasp IN1222) and other admissible sites had no dedicated Castanea mollissima page and were not used.

Not applicable to this tree outdoors: humidity, indoor temperature, light in foot-candles, watering intervals, fertilizing schedule; no admissible source gives them, left null. chill_damage_f null: NC State and MoBot give hardiness zones (4a-8b; 4 to 8), which are not damage-onset temperatures.

attracts_pollinators left null: NC State says the nut attracts wild life and carries a #wildlife friendly tag, and describes cross-pollination between trees, but no source names bees, butterflies or other pollinators attracted.

MoBot's Uses text, read in a browser by the auditor and not cited because MoBot refuses connections from this machine (ConnectError), warns: "Unfortunately, as is the case with the fruit of the sweet gum but perhaps more so, falling chestnuts can pose a significant litter problem, and often make walking barefoot in the lawn a real adventure." records.name_note: Sources lead with different names. NC State's dedicated Juglans regia page has a bare-binomial H1. Its page-title parenthetical and its rendered Common Name(s) list (alphabetized, same order) both read Black Sea Walnut, Common Walnut, English Walnut, Persian Walnut, so the list leads with Black Sea Walnut, and its description opens 'English Walnut is a broadleaf deciduous tree'. RHS's Juglans regia (F) page gives 'common walnut' under its H1 and lists English walnut and Persian walnut among its other common names. English Walnut was kept as the display name because NC State's description opens with it; Common Walnut (RHS) and Black Sea Walnut (NC State's list lead) are equally dedicated-page leads. Persian Walnut appears on both pages. Carpathian Walnut appears on neither as a name for the species (NC State lists 'Carpathian' only as a cultivar entry).
unknowns: toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail left null: the dedicated NC State Juglans regia page carries no cat/dog toxicity statement and no moldy-hull or moldy-nut warning, and the RHS page has none either. The PSU and UMD juglone pages and the UGA pages found in search are genus-level or black-walnut pages, so they were not used for this species.

Allergy / edibility: NC State states unconditionally 'The nuts are edible. They may be eaten fresh, roasted, and salted.' No admissible dedicated page addresses the hull or leaf as food or as a hazard, so is_edible=true rests on the nuts only.

Allelopathy (kept separate from black walnut, whose page was not consulted or copied): NC State's English Walnut page says 'The roots of this tree produce a chemical known as juglones. This chemical is toxic to other plants including azaleas, rhododendron, blueberries, peonies, tomatoes, peppers, and potatoes.' It gives no comparison to black walnut and no strength figure, so nothing about lower juglone output is recorded. This sentence concerns other plants, not pets.

Missouri Botanical Garden / plantfinder.mobot.org page (kempercode a876) could not be loaded: the fetch failed with a TLS certificate error through the proxy, so no MoBot data is used. Not cached or repaired.

RHS: the only RHS page found is titled 'Juglans regia (F)' (the '(F)' is part of the page title; common name 'common walnut'). Its Max Height 'Higher than 12 metres' and Max Spread 'wider than 8 metres' are open-ended, so they give no usable bound and the sizes come from NC State alone. RHS lists pH as acid, alkaline or neutral and moisture as 'Moist but well-drained or Well-drained'. Because RHS accepts acid and alkaline soils, soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max are left null despite NC State's Neutral (6.0-8.0) band.

water_regime left null: NC State gives only the soil-drainage tags (Good Drainage, Moist) and a soil-preference sentence, and RHS gives only a soil description. Neither states a watering rule. NC State also says the tree is intolerant of 'poor or wet soils', so soil_drainage is read as moderate (moist but well-drained).

outdoor_sun_exposure: NC State (structured Light field, tags #full sun, #shade intolerant, and prose) and RHS Position (Full sun) agree on full sun only. direct_sun_hours_max left null because the only hour figure is in NC State's generic light-category field.

attracts_pollinators is null: NC State's structured Attracts field names Moths and Small Mammals, but its Wildlife Value text ties the moths to larval-host use (Hickory horndevil and Luna moth) and says 'Adult Hickory Horndevil moths do not feed'; neither NC State nor RHS makes any pollinator statement. Set at landing (the research record had true as a 'weak positive').
is_houseplant=false is inferred from NC State's statement that it is an ornamental tree best planted in a large landscape area; no source discusses indoor culture.

No dedicated page from UF/IFAS, Clemson, PSU, UMD or UGA for Juglans regia was found, so those hosts contribute nothing. Temperature tolerance: NC State lists USDA zones 3a-7b, which is a hardiness range and not a damage-onset temperature, so chill_damage_f is null. Fertilizing and humidity are not addressed by NC State or RHS.

records.name_note: NC State's dedicated page has the bare binomial as its H1. Its rendered Common Name(s) list is alphabetized and matches the page-title parenthetical: Juneberry, Pidgeon berry, Saskatoon Serviceberry, Western serviceberry, Western Shadbush. Juneberry is the first item. The page's description calls the plant 'The Saskatoon serviceberry'. Saskatoon Serviceberry, the third alphabetized list entry and the description's name, is the display name, chosen because NC State also lists Juneberry for Amelanchier canadensis (Shadblow Serviceberry) and Juneberries for A. arborea (Downy Serviceberry). Those are separate species and are not merged here.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's description says: "The leaves contain cyanide and can be fatal to animals if consumed in large quantities." It names no animal species (neither cats nor dogs), so this is not scored as pet toxicity. The page carries no Poison block and no Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tags, and it states no seed warning. Edibility on the same page: the structured Edibility field says "The fruit is edible" (Fruit Value To Gardener: Edible), so edibility is fruit-only and the leaves are the part with the cyanide statement. The page gives no cooked-versus-raw instruction.
unknowns: Only one admissible source gave a dedicated page for this exact name: NC State Plant Toolbox (plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/amelanchier-alnifolia/). RHS lists only varieties (A. alnifolia var. alnifolia, var. cusickii), which are not this exact taxon, so no RHS species page, Name Status, pH or size data was used.

MoBot (www.missouribotanicalgarden.org / plantfinder.mobot.org) could not be fetched in this session (ConnectError, and a certificate error via curl), so it was not checked. EDIS, Clemson HGIC, Penn State, UMD and UGA were tried or not found: Clemson returned 403, the EDIS and PSU pages were not reachable or not found, and the UMD serviceberry page does not mention A. alnifolia. None was cited.

toxic_to_pets is null: the only toxicity sentence (leaves contain cyanide, can be fatal to 'animals') names no animal, so it does not support a cat/dog verdict. No source found states a seed cyanogenic warning for this taxon, so none is recorded.
is_edible is true for the fruit only (NC State Edibility field). The leaves carry a cyanide statement on the same page. NC State does not say whether the fruit is eaten raw or cooked.

outdoor_sun_exposure is full_sun and part_shade, from NC State's structured Light field (Full sun; Partial Shade) and its tags '#full sun tolerant' and '#partial shade tolerant'. The Light field also lists 'Deep shade (Less than 2 hours to no direct sunlight)'. It is not mapped to full_shade because the page's tags carry no shade tag, the prose says the best berries come in full sun, and the only broader light statement is the tolerance clause 'Easily tolerates a variety of moisture, soil, and light conditions.' direct_sun_hours_max is null because the only hour figures on the page are the site-wide light-category legend.
soil_ph_max is null: NC State gives only the band 'Neutral (6.0-8.0)' and no RHS pH field was available to check whether alkaline soils are acceptable. soil_ph_min 6.0 is the lower edge of that band.

soil_drainage moderate rests on NC State's Soil Drainage tags Good Drainage, Occasionally Dry and Occasionally Wet (spanning both dry and wet). The description also says it 'Easily tolerates a variety of moisture, soil, and light conditions' and is drought and salt tolerant; that is a tolerance statement, not a watering instruction, so water_regime is null.

Size: NC State's Dimensions block gives Height 3 ft 0 in to 18 ft 0 in and Width 6 ft 0 in to 10 ft 0 in (converted to 36-216 and 72-120 inches). The description prose differs slightly (3-18 feet tall and 6-8 feet, up to 30 feet in rich moist soils; the Stem Description says up to 30 ft). The structured block was used. Cultivar sizes on the page were not used.

is_houseplant false: NC State does not address indoor culture; its Plant Type field lists Perennial, Shrub and Tree and it gives USDA zones 4a-9b. Humidity, indoor temperature, light in foot-candles, chill damage, watering cadence and fertilizer are null because no admissible source for this taxon states them.
NC State's USDA zone tag runs 4a through 9b; this is a hardiness range, not a damage-onset temperature, so chill_damage_f is null.

Eight species: Beefsteak Plant, Chicory, Cobnut, Black Elder, Caribbean Oregano, Chinese Chestnut, English Walnut, Saskatoon Serviceberry. Coleus amboinicus lands as Caribbean Oregano, the first item of the only readable dedicated page's rendered list (Cuban Oregano is its second item and the description's 'other common name'); accepted name left null as researched (NC State titles it Plectranthus amboinicus and lists Coleus amboinicus as 'Previously known as').
